title: Attitudes, Beliefs and Social Cognition
summary: Attitudes are favourable or unfavourable evaluations of people, objects, ideas and situations, expressed with words such as like, dislike, love, hate, good and bad. Three components: cognitive (thinking that produces beliefs about the attitude object), affective (direction and intensity of feeling or emotion) and behavioural (likelihood of acting in a certain way). The components may be inconsistent, but in a strong attitude they are consistent. Attitudes are held for a long time, change with new experiences, and differ in type and strength between persons.

(1) They help us understand the world (positive attitudes bring us closer to people, role models such as Sachin Tendulkar and Mother Teresa). (2) They describe the social groups we belong to (shared attitudes bind family, religious or political groups). (3) They express our values and self-concept, i.e. identity (Gandhi's honesty). (4) They help us get support, praise and acceptance from others, since people with similar attitudes attract each other.

Learnt through four kinds of learning: direct contact (classical conditioning, e.g. a child dislikes sprouts and generalises the dislike), direct instruction (parents, teachers and leaders, e.g. not to smoke), interaction with others (adopting the group's attitudes; rewards from peers act as instrumental learning) and observational learning (grandparents' bhajans, mother's fear of a stray dog). Education, media, TV, movies and advertisements also shape attitudes.

Attitudes are hard to change but can change with new learning. Source (communicator): more change if the communicator is an expert, trustworthy, attractive and similar to the receiver. Message: clear and well organised; messages that produce anxiety and fear are more effective. Person (target): strong, personally important, complex and interconnected attitudes are difficult to change (attitude to family versus preference for a soap). 'Who says what to whom' decides change; advertisers use all three. Congruent change (in the same direction as the existing attitude) is easier than incongruent change.

People often say one thing and do another (want to be fit but do not exercise). Attitudes predict behaviour when they are strong and consistent, when the person is conscious of the attitude and can recall it easily, when formed through direct experience, when external or social pressure is minimal, and when the behaviour is planned and personally relevant (which college to join) rather than spontaneous.
Beliefs are the acceptance of something as truth (belief in a supernatural power or afterlife); strong beliefs become unshakable and help us organise experiences and predict behaviour and events.

Social cognition is the interpretation, analysis and remembering of information from the social world so that we think, feel and understand about people. To manage too much information we form schemas: sets of interconnected beliefs, information and examples about social objects, events and people (person schemas, event schemas, role schemas); they guide thinking and behaviour. Heuristics are simple rules for quick complex decisions (the 'professor' stereotype). Attribution is looking for causes of one's own and others' behaviour: internal (personal) causes like effort, or external causes like a tough paper. Fundamental attribution error: we explain others' behaviour by internal causes and our own by external causes. Biases: optimistic bias (we expect more positive events than others), negativity bias (greater weight to negative information), counterfactual thinking ('what might have been'), confirmatory bias (seeking information that supports one's beliefs), ignoring base-rate information, thought suppression (preventing oneself from thinking of certain topics). Errors arise when we use heuristics for unimportant events; important events call for conscious processing. Biases still help us adapt by focusing on important information.

objective: A favourable or unfavourable evaluation of people, objects, ideas and situations.
Name the three components of attitude.

vsa: They simplify a complicated social world, help understand people and events, define groups and identity and win acceptance.
How do attitudes help in identity?
They express a person's values and self-concept, e.g. Gandhi's honesty or Mother Teresa's concern for the poor.
We adopt the group's attitudes, and praise and approval from friends reward and strengthen them (instrumental learning).
Why is an expert more effective in changing attitudes?
An expert, trustworthy, attractive and similar communicator is believed more, so the receiver changes attitude.
Give one reason why attitude may not predict behaviour.
Social or peer pressure, e.g. a boy who dislikes drinking does so because of friends.
Simple rules used to make complex decisions quickly, such as identifying a 'professor' from typical attributes.
Internal attribution explains an outcome by personal causes such as effort; external attribution by outside causes such as a tough paper.
sa: Explain the three components of attitude with an example.
Cognitive (belief that the neighbour is intelligent), affective (liking or disliking his manners) and behavioural (helping him when needed). In strong attitudes the three are consistent.
They help us understand the world and choose whom to approach, describe our social groups, express our identity and values, and win support and acceptance from others.
By direct contact (conditioning), direct instruction by parents and teachers, interaction with others (group and reward), observational learning from models, and through education and media.
Explain the factors of attitude change.
Source: expert, trustworthy, attractive, similar. Message: clear, organised, fear-arousing. Person: strong, complex, important attitudes resist change; advertisers use all three.
Explain the relationship between attitude and behaviour.
It is complex; attitudes predict behaviour when strong and consistent, accessible, based on direct experience, free of social pressure and when behaviour is planned and personally relevant.
Describe the fundamental attribution error and any two biases.
We attribute others' acts to internal causes and our own to external causes. Optimistic bias expects good events for oneself; negativity bias gives more weight to negative information.
la: Define attitude, describe its components and functions.

Attitude is a favourable or unfavourable evaluation of people, objects and situations. Components: cognitive, affective and behavioural. Functions: understanding the world, defining groups, expressing identity and values, and gaining acceptance and support.
Explain how attitudes are formed and changed.

Formed by direct contact, instruction, interaction with others and observation, and by media. Change depends on source (expert, trustworthy), message (clear, fear-arousing) and person (strong attitudes resist). Congruent change is easier than incongruent.
Explain the relationship between attitude and behaviour with the conditions for a strong relationship.

Attitude and behaviour often differ (wanting fitness but not exercising). A strong link exists when attitudes are strong, consistent, easily recalled, formed by direct experience, free of social pressure, and when behaviour is planned and personally relevant.
Define social cognition. Explain schemas, heuristics, attribution and biases.

Social cognition is interpreting and remembering social information. Schemas organise information (person, event, role); heuristics give quick decisions; attribution seeks internal or external causes; errors include fundamental attribution error, optimistic bias, negativity bias, counterfactual thinking, confirmatory bias and thought suppression.
